Joan of Arc, known as Jeanne d'Arc, was a French military leader and saint who played a pivotal role in defending France during the later stages of the Hundred Years War. Born a peasant girl in eastern France, she claimed divine guidance and led French forces to crucial victories against English occupation. Her remarkable military career, trial for heresy, and martyrdom at the stake made her a national symbol of French resistance and spiritual conviction.

Born around 1412 in the village of Domremy in eastern France to a peasant family with no military background or connections, Joan claimed to receive visions and divine voices from saints, instructing her to lead France to victory during a period of military defeat and occupation. She convinced the weak French dauphin, later known as Charles VII, of her divine mission and secured command of an army despite her youth and gender. Her most celebrated victory came at Orleans in 1429, where she rallied French forces along the Loire River and turned the tide of the Hundred Years War. But her fortune reversed when Burgundian forces captured her and sold her to the English, who tried her for heresy and witchcraft in 1431. Burned at the stake in Rouen that same year at age nineteen, she became a martyr, later canonized as a saint and national heroine of France. Her brief military career lasted only about a year and a half, yet it fundamentally shifted the momentum of a war that had lasted nearly a century. The trial record is one of the best-documented medieval proceedings and provides insight into medieval warfare, gender roles, and religious belief. She became an enduring symbol of French nationalism, female heroism, and religious conviction, her legacy influencing literature, art, and political thought for centuries to come.
